answer_text:
# 💜 The History of Purple

---

## From the Sea to the Throne — A Colour Like No Other

Of all the colours that have wound their way through human history, none has a story quite as dramatic, as costly, or as transformative as **purple**. It is a colour that has commanded empires, bankrupted the ambitious, and been reborn in a laboratory accident. It is, in every sense, the colour of power.

---

## I. The Phoenician Origin — A Colour Born from the Sea

The story begins around 3,000 years ago with the Phoenicians, a seafaring civilisation living along the Mediterranean coast, in what is now modern Lebanon, Syria, and Israel.

Tyrian purple may first have been used by the ancient Phoenicians as early as 1570 BC. It has even been suggested that the name *Phoenicia* itself means "land of purple."

The dye's origins were anything but glamorous. It stemmed from the foul-smelling mucous gland of a marine mollusc. As a result, the very term "purple" owes itself to the Latin word for a purple shellfish: *purpura*. A time-consuming process saw these sea snails dried and boiled to make Tyrian dye — many of the creatures were needed to dye even a small segment of fabric, but the benefits meant that the intensity of the colour was long-lasting and not prone to fade.

Just how many snails were needed? About 250,000 snails were required to make an ounce of purple dye. Tyrian purple was therefore extraordinarily rare and expensive, making purple clothing ruinously costly — a pound of purple wool cost more than a year's salary.

The dye was greatly prized in antiquity because the colour did not easily fade, but instead became brighter with weathering and sunlight. It came in various shades, the most prized being that of black-tinted clotted blood.

---

## II. The Imperial Colour — Rome, Byzantium, and the Divine Right to Wear Purple

The stratospheric price of purple made it a symbol of status unlike any other in the ancient world. Deemed decadent and valuable, purple was reserved only for the elite, including rulers, high-ranking religious clergy, and those of royal rank. In Ancient Greece, legislation stated that the higher your status, the greater your right to wear purple.

In Rome, the colour became a tool of political theatre. The most senior Roman magistrates wore a *toga praetexta*, a white toga edged in Tyrian purple. The even more sumptuous *toga picta*, solid Tyrian purple with gold thread edging, was worn by generals celebrating a Roman triumph.

By the fourth century AD, sumptuary laws in Rome had been tightened so much that only the Roman emperor was permitted to wear Tyrian purple. As a result, "purple" is sometimes used as a metonym for the office — the phrase "donned the purple" means "became emperor."

Third-century Roman emperor Aurelian famously wouldn't allow his wife to buy a shawl made from Tyrian purple silk because it literally cost its weight in gold.

The Byzantine Empire took this veneration even further. Empresses would give birth in a room called a *porphyry*, a prized purple stone chamber in the Great Palace of Constantinople. Their children were therefore "born to the purple" — coining the phrase that now refers to anyone born of high and noble birth.

---

## III. The Middle Ages — A Lost Secret

For over a thousand years, Tyrian purple was the most prestigious dye in the world. But by the Middle Ages, it started to disappear. The Byzantine Empire, which had controlled the dye trade, declined. The technique of making the dye was kept secret, passed down within families, and eventually lost. Cheaper dyes made from plants became more practical. By the time of the Renaissance, the original recipe for Tyrian purple was forgotten — people knew it had once existed, but nobody knew how to make it anymore.

Yet the *idea* of purple endured. In the medieval Church, purple was prominently used during Lent and Advent, periods of reflection and preparation. Purple liturgical vestments worn by clergy symbolised penance, humility, and mourning, capturing the spirit of introspection that these seasons demand.

---

## IV. The Tudor Obsession — Purple as Law

The colour's legal power reached its most extreme expression during the Tudor period. In Elizabethan Europe, purple was reserved for royalty, and throughout England's Tudor period only King Henry VIII was allowed to dress in the colour — he went as far as committing an Earl to death by treason for wearing it.

Everyone in England had to abide by Sumptuary Laws, which strictly regulated what colours, fabrics and clothes could and couldn't be worn by different classes within society. Queen Elizabeth I's Sumptuary Laws forbade anyone but close relatives of the royal family to wear purple, so the colour not only reflected the wearer's wealth but also their regal status.

---

## V. The Accident That Changed Everything — Mauve, 1856

It wasn't until the 19th century that purple made a comeback. In 1856, an 18-year-old chemistry student named William Henry Perkin accidentally created the first synthetic purple dye while trying to make a medicine for malaria. He called it mauveine.

Perkin was at the time trying to synthesize quinine in a laboratory. When cleaning up the solution he'd created with alcohol, he noticed he'd produced a dark purple liquid. He initially labelled it Tyrian purple, to capitalise on history. He soon switched to calling it *mauve*, after the French name for the mallow flower.

His purple dyestuff marked the beginning of a revolution in organic chemistry — the birth of an industry that has since given us a rainbow of colours, as well as drugs, explosives, fertilizers, plastics, and synthetics beyond measure.

The new colour quickly became fashionable, particularly after Queen Victoria wore a silk gown dyed with mauveine to the Royal Exhibition of 1862. Prior to Perkin's discovery, mauve was a colour only the aristocracy and rich could afford to wear. Perkin developed an industrial process, built a factory, and produced the dye by the ton, so almost anyone could wear mauve. It was the first of a series of modern industrial dyes which completely transformed both the chemical industry and fashion.

---

## VI. Art, Revolution, and Rock 'n' Roll

During the Impressionist era, the phrase *"violettomania"* was bounced about — representing the fervour of artists who had a fashion for embellishing canvases with a violet tinting, such as Monet, who preferred to use violet over black to better portray light and shade.

In the 20th century, purple's story became one of duality — regal yet rebellious. George VI wore purple in his official portrait, and it was prominent in every feature of the coronation of Elizabeth II in 1953,
